generalizedRange: Virunga Massif and Bwindi, East-Central Africa
hook: The only great ape whose numbers are rising.

story.text: A mountain gorilla family moves through the cold high forest together: infants riding on backs, a silverback leading from the center.
Their hair is longer and thicker than any other gorilla's, grown for volcano slopes where nights can drop below freezing.
Each one can be told apart by its nose print, unique as a human fingerprint.
Their entire world is less than three hundred square miles, split between the Virunga volcanoes and the Bwindi forest.
The dangers are human-sized: snares set for other animals, and our illnesses — sharing most of our DNA, gorillas can catch flu, pneumonia, even Ebola.
In 1981, the Virunga population had crashed to 242, and extinction by the year 2000 was a serious prediction.
Then came four decades of daily protection: trackers walking to the gorillas every single morning, veterinarians treating snared animals where they lie.
The count now stands above one thousand and keeps rising — the only great ape population on Earth that is growing.
To witness the mountain gorilla is to see what protection, held steadily for a generation, can actually do.
The recovery holds only as long as the choices behind it — funded rangers, careful tourism, forests left standing.

editorial.notes: Card v2 drafted from verified WWF-UK, AWF, Fossey Fund, and Gorilla Doctors pages. Population 1,063 is the WWF-UK phrasing of the 2016/2018 census (604 Virunga + 459 Bwindi-Sarambwe). Region circles are cartographic generalizations of whole national parks.

stats.diet: Leaves, shoots & stems — up to 40 lbs a day

reproduction.text: After a gestation of about eight and a half months, a newborn weighs under four pounds — half the weight of a human baby. Mothers have their first infant between ten and twelve, and nurse each one for over three years.

insight.text: A mountain gorilla's high-tannin diet stains its teeth almost black — the same compounds that darken tea and coffee.

programs.title: Daily protection
programs.summary: Teams of more than a hundred expert trackers walk to the gorillas every day, directly protecting about half of Rwanda's mountain gorillas.

programs.title: Wild veterinary care
programs.summary: The only veterinary team treating wild eastern gorillas, monitoring nearly 800 habituated gorillas and freeing snared animals with a 98% survival rate.
